_doc: Closing self-assessment statements per chapter (teacher 2026-11-06: more varied than 'I learned to …'). They replace the chapter's goals at the end of Check your understanding. scripts/inquiry.py sa_goals_html.
fy3-1: I understand why force tells the strength of an interaction and how a force meter measures it.
I can tell weight and mass apart, also in everyday speech.
I can calculate an object's weight on Earth and on other celestial bodies.
fy3-2: I can recognise when a force does work and when it does not.
I can calculate work both with the formula and as the area under a graph.
I know what power tells and can compare the power of two devices.
fy3-3: I can describe the state of a gas with its temperature, pressure and volume.
I understand with the particle model what pressure and temperature are.
I can justify why temperatures are compared in kelvins.
fy3-4: I understand how the same force can cause a large or a small pressure.
I can calculate the pressure of a liquid at different depths.
I can read both the constant term and the slope of a pressure-depth graph.
fy3-5: I can tell heat, work and internal energy apart.
I can use the first law of thermodynamics as energy bookkeeping.
I notice when the everyday word 'heat' means something else in physics.
fy3-6: I can calculate the heat that warms a substance.
I understand what specific heat capacity tells about a substance.
I can solve the equilibrium temperature of a calorimeter with energy conservation.
fy3-7: I understand where the energy goes when the temperature stays constant during a change of phase.
I can calculate the heat needed for melting and vaporisation.
I can recognise the stages of a change of phase in a heating curve.
fy3-8: I can explain with the particle model why a solid expands when it warms.
I can plan an experiment to find out what the change in length depends on.
I can calculate the change in an object's length and volume.
fy3-9: I can use Boyle's law in an isothermal process.
I can show with a graph that pressure is inversely proportional to volume.
I understand how the volume of a gas depends on its kelvin temperature.
fy3-10: I can infer from pressure, volume and temperature how much gas there is.
I can use the ideal gas law.
I understand gas pressure as particles colliding with the walls.
fy3-11: I can calculate the work of an expanding gas and see it as the area under a graph.
I understand why a heat engine cannot turn all heat into work.
I can calculate the efficiency of a heat engine.
fy3-12: I can recognise conduction, convection and thermal radiation in everyday situations.
I can calculate the heat flow through a wall or a window.
I can explain the greenhouse effect with the energy balance.
fy3-13: I can turn measurement data into a straight line and extend it.
I can determine absolute zero from my own measurements.
I can estimate the uncertainty of a result with the steepest and the shallowest line.
fy3-14: I understand why ice cools a drink so effectively.
I can decide by comparing amounts of heat whether all the ice melts.
I can calculate the equilibrium temperature when part of a substance melts.
fy3-15: I can calculate the efficiency of a power plant chain from the efficiencies of its stages.
I know where the largest energy loss of a condensing power plant occurs.
I understand why combined heat and power makes better use of the fuel.
fy3-16: I can combine several heat phenomena into one energy balance.
I can justify whether energy goes into warming or into a change of phase.
I dare to take on a multi-step everyday heat problem.
